newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pope urges Bosnian rivals to forgive.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges Bosnian rivals to forgive.

text.p: Pope John Paul urged Bosnia's hostile communities on Sunday to seek reconciliation and renounce the religious hatreds which plunged the country into Europe's worst war for half a century.
Shivering in the wintry chill at a snowswept football stadium where he celebrated mass, the 76-year-old Pontiff told worshippers:

"Let us forgive and let us ask for forgiveness...We cannot fail to undertake the difficult but necessary pilgrimage of forgiveness, which leads to a profound reconciliation," he told worshippers at a Sarajevo stadium.
The Pope flew to Sarajevo on Saturday in defiance of an apparent assassination threat. Police dismantled more than a score of anti-tank mines planted on his route from the airport to the city centre.

Bosnian police and NATO peacekeepers immediately stepped up security measures in the capital shared by Moslems, Roman Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs trying to keep the flame of Bosnian multi-ethnicity alive.
Police had no indication of who was responsible for the threat to the Pope, who narrowly escaped death when he was shot by a Turkish gunman in St Peter's Square in 1981.

"It is worrying. We are looking into the details of that now but it is still too early to make a definite assessment of what it was," Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to Bosnia, told reporters.
Some 35,000 people braved wind and snow to attend the Papal mass in Kosevo stadium, waving yellow and white banners upon the Pope's arrival.
Five hundred buses ferried pilgrims from across Bosnia and neighbouring Croatia to see the first visit by a Pope to the Bosnian capital.
Only 20,000 Croats -- less than 10 percent of the city's population -- still live in Sarajevo.
Mourning Sarajevo's plight during the brutal wartime siege, the Pope questioned whether Europe had done enough to try to end the Yugoslav conflict.
"Europe took part in it (the war) as a witness. But we must ask ourselves: was it always a fully responsible witness? This question cannot be avoided."
During the mass, the Pope's left hand shook in what is widely regarded as a sign that he has Parkinson's disease.
Asked if the Pope was suffering from the cold, Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said, "He is more accustomed to this than to the sun."
The Papal visit came at a time of tense relations inside the country's Moslem-Croat Federation, which together with a Serb republic comprises post-war Bosnia.

The Pope, prevented from visiting Sarajevo during the war because Serbs refused to guarantee his safety, earlier met Moslem, Croat and Serb members of the new collective presidency amid tight security.
The Vatican said the Moslem chairman of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, had sent a letter to Bosnian Cardinal Vinko Puljic saying he was "sad" to learn about the explosives discovered by police.

Speaking at the national museum building which still bears scars from the 1992-95 war, the Pope urged political leaders to build dialogue among Bosnian Moslems, Catholic Croats and Orthodox Christian Serbs.
The peacetime inter-ethnic government has been virtually paralysed, with politicians from each community unable to agree on the most basic issues.
The Pope carried his message of reconciliation to leaders of other religions, including Metropolitan Nikolaj of the Orthodox Serbian Church,
After embracing, the Pope and Nikolaj held 20 minutes of talks. Nikolaj gave the Pope an icon of the Madonna as a gift.
"This is a special gift from my people and from me personally, asking her to hear our prayers and bring us peace," said Nikolaj, whose church backed hardline Serb nationalists during the war.
Serb leaders resent the Vatican for its early recognition of the breakaway republics of Croatia and Bosnia during the fighting which accompanied the collapse of old Yugoslavia.
